dateNote: AWS lab and subsequent incident-response and release-testing work: 2026.
name: KubeVista
alt: KubeVista’s isometric cluster station showing robot workloads, service routing, telemetry, and cloud infrastructure
summary: A Kubernetes console for investigating failed workloads, reviewing a fix, and checking recovery. Built around an EKS platform I deployed on AWS.
detail: I built the Go API, React console, and AWS platform around them. The console connects Deployments, ReplicaSets, Pods, and events so an investigation can lead into a reviewed restart, scale, or rollback. Recovery checks look at the rollout—not just whether Kubernetes accepted the request.
bullets: Restart, scale, and rollback are limited by namespace, Deployment, and replica guardrails.
Every change requires a reason, Kubernetes dry run, current resource version, and single-use review plan.
Production execution verifies the load balancer's signed identity claims and records an audit receipt.
All 896 requests returned HTTP 200 during a 45-second AWS pod-loss test; the replacement became Ready in two seconds.
note: The original AWS lab has been torn down. Guarded operations, incident recovery, and blue-green release checks were tested separately in disposable kind clusters and merged into main.

ownership.scope: Product, Go API, React interface, AWS platform, delivery, security boundaries, and operations
ownership.status: Incident and blue-green release labs merged; AWS environment retired

architecture.alt: KubeVista architecture from GitHub Actions through Argo CD into a private EKS node group, with AWS ingress, pod identity, secrets, and an observability stack
architecture.caption: The original AWS platform. The newer operator path adds reviewed restart, scale, and rollback without granting arbitrary cluster writes.
architecture.how: Terraform provisioned networking across three availability zones, two private worker nodes, Pod Identity, and KMS encryption. Twelve Argo CD applications delivered the platform, with metrics, logs, and traces through Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, and OpenTelemetry. The newer Go operator path checks identity, dry-runs the change, and follows rollout state after execution.
decisions: The browser never submits YAML. Restart, scale, and rollback are typed operations; rollback pins the reviewed template from an owned ReplicaSet.
Review plans expire after five minutes, work once, and are bound to the request and Kubernetes resource version to prevent edits or replay.

Recovery requires the expected controller generation and updated/available replicas. A local kind lab exercises probe, crash-loop, image-pull, memory, and scheduling failures. Plans and receipts remain process-local.
A blue-green release lab validates a candidate before switching Service traffic, checks latency and errors, and rolls back without overwriting a concurrent Service edit.

caseStudy.title: How a change gets through
caseStudy.intro: The write path is deliberately narrower than the inventory API. Each stage removes a class of accidental or unauthorized change before Kubernetes accepts it.

steps.title: Choose
steps.text: Select restart, scale, or rollback for an allowed Deployment and explain why the change is needed.

steps.title: Constrain
steps.text: The API rejects unsupported kinds, namespaces, actions, and replica counts before touching the cluster.

steps.title: Dry run
steps.text: Kubernetes authorization and admission evaluate the same request without persisting it.

steps.title: Bind
steps.text: A five-minute, single-use plan locks the reviewed request to the current resource version.

steps.title: Execute
steps.text: The API rechecks identity and dry run, applies the scoped change, records a receipt, and checks rollout recovery.

architecture.outcome: All 896 AWS test requests returned HTTP 200 while an API pod was replaced; its replacement became Ready within two seconds. Separate kind labs exercise five failure classes and guarded blue-green releases, with 20 desktop/mobile browser tests covering the console.

name: Illuma
summary: A college admissions platform for researching schools, reviewing essays, and building a college list.
detail: I founded Illuma to bring college research, planning, and essay feedback into one workspace. I built the platform and its typed AI tools, then traced a slow streaming workflow to database writes that were making the model wait on progress updates.
bullets: 39 typed tools with shared state and deterministic validation.
Admissions modeling across 130 universities.
79,000 applicant outcomes underpin the platform.
Grew to more than 5,000 users.
note: The platform has 39 typed tools and admissions modeling across 130 universities. Product figures in my September 2026 résumé: 5,000+ users, $10K+ revenue, and 4M+ organic social views.

ownership.scope: Product, typed AI tools, admissions model, backend performance, and platform implementation

architecture.alt: Illuma architecture showing a student workspace, an agent coordinator, research and writing tools, shared state and validation, and admissions data and prediction services
architecture.caption: A coordinated tool system: each specialist works against the same student context instead of producing isolated chat responses.
architecture.how: A student request enters a coordinator that selects typed tools for school research, college-list planning, or essay review. Every tool reads and updates shared application state, and deterministic checks gate what can move to the next step. The prediction path combines a student profile with historical applicant outcomes and university data.
decisions: Typed tool inputs and outputs make handoffs inspectable and reject malformed results early.
Shared state keeps recommendations consistent across research, essays, and the evolving college list.
Admissions prediction is kept as a separate data pipeline rather than hidden inside an unconstrained language-model answer.
Progress updates are coalesced in a background writer. Conditional database updates protect completed results from late progress writes, while final results are saved separately.
architecture.outcome: Progress-callback overhead fell from 318 seconds to 23 milliseconds in a before/after staging comparison. The fix is deployed; these timings describe that sample, not a production latency guarantee.

dateNote: Original build: March–July 2026. Transaction and recovery improvements shipped September 2026.
name: Ledgly
alt: Ledgly financial dashboard with charges, payments, and membership balances
summary: A shared ledger that helps club treasurers match payment emails to dues. Fewer spreadsheet detective stories.
detail: A club ledger should not create a second payment because someone clicked twice. I built the financial model and reconciliation workflow, then added idempotent writes, concurrency-safe allocations, durable email jobs, and recovery tests for the less cooperative days.
bullets: Gmail ingestion matches payment notices to members and records confidence for review.
Organization-scoped roles are enforced by the API.
The assistant proposes financial changes for confirmation before executing them.
Before-and-after audit records support batch undo and redo.
note: The reliability changes are merged and deployed. Gmail ingestion and notification delivery have separate activation flags; deployment does not mean those workers are enabled. Ledgly records payments; it does not move money.

ownership.scope: Architecture, ledger model, reconciliation, permissions, and audit workflow
ownership.status: Reliability changes deployed; background workers separately controlled

architecture.alt: Ledgly architecture showing the Next.js interface, NestJS API, PostgreSQL ledger, Gmail ingestion, and a review gate before financial records are changed
architecture.caption: Incoming payment email becomes a proposed ledger match, not an automatic financial fact.
architecture.how: The Next.js interface calls an organization-scoped NestJS API backed by Prisma and PostgreSQL. Durable Gmail jobs discover and process payment notices, with sender matching and confidence scores for review. Imports commit atomically. A transactional outbox records notification work alongside database changes, then retries delivery per destination.
decisions: Amounts use integer cents. Serializable allocation transactions and bounded retries prevent competing requests from overallocating a payment or charge.
An organization-scoped idempotency key binds to the request fingerprint. The payment, audit entry, and replay response commit together; changed-payload reuse is rejected.
Durable ingestion jobs and notification outbox entries survive process restarts. Replay is audited, and ambiguous payment matches and AI financial writes still require review.
architecture.outcome: Tests terminate a worker after payment commit, restart the database, and restore a backup before redelivery, checking that the payment is not duplicated. External notification delivery can still repeat after an ambiguous provider acknowledgment.

dateNote: Original project dates. Performance and accessibility updates: September 2026.
name: Sizzle
summary: Recipes with an interactive kitchen counter. The ingredients have actual physics.
detail: A dish or a few ingredients become a saved recipe and an illustrated cooking view. I built the generation pipeline and physics counter, then separated frame-by-frame movement from React rendering so the playful part does not keep rerendering the app.
note: The performance and accessibility upgrade is tested on codex/cooking-performance, not production-deployed. The benchmark is a local React rendering measurement, not an FPS or CPU claim.
bullets: Structured ingredients, equipment, and steps drive the interface.
Matter.js handles gravity, collisions, and ingredient placement.
Supabase stores recipes; OCI Object Storage holds the generated step illustrations.

ownership.scope: Recipe pipeline, FastAPI service, interactive cooking view, and OCI deployment
ownership.status: Performance and accessibility upgrade tested on a feature branch

architecture.alt: Sizzle pipeline from a dish or ingredient prompt through recipe lookup and structured generation to Supabase, image jobs, OCI Object Storage, and a Matter.js cooking view
architecture.caption: The recipe is usable before the slower illustration jobs finish.
architecture.how: A natural-language request first searches saved recipes. If nothing fits, FastAPI creates structured ingredients, equipment, and steps, persists them in Supabase, and starts illustration work in the background. The Next.js cooking view renders each step and uses Matter.js to place the relevant objects on a virtual counter.
decisions: Recipe generation produces a fixed structure so the interface does not have to parse prose.
Illustrations run in a bounded, in-process worker pool after saving the recipe. This is background work, not a durable job queue.
Matter.js updates element transforms through refs; React owns recipe state. A single runner pauses when hidden or paused, with keyboard movement and a static reduced-motion layout.
architecture.outcome: With 20 items, React commits fell from 301 to zero over a five-second development sample while physics movement continued. Browser checks cover pause, keyboard controls, reduced motion, and runtime errors without paid APIs.

dateNote: Original project dates. Session isolation and versioned retrieval improvements: September 2026.
name: Academis
videoAlt: Academis demo moving from the AP Economics study desk into the Biology course workspace
summary: An AP study workspace that brings textbook retrieval, tutoring, quizzes, and graphs together.
detail: I built Academis around course documents so tutoring has something concrete to refer to. The latest work tracks where each passage came from, keeps retrieval within the selected course and document version, and declines to answer when usable evidence is missing.
note: Versioned retrieval and source references are implemented and tested on codex/retrieval-provenance. Live Atlas ingestion and retrieval-threshold calibration remain before rollout. Economics has the most complete content; science courses remain partial.
bullets: PDF extraction, chunking, and embeddings feed MongoDB Atlas Vector Search.
FastAPI separates tutoring, retrieval, quiz generation, and graph generation.
Firebase Authentication protects student routes.

ownership.scope: Document ingestion, retrieval, tutoring API, and study interface
ownership.status: Versioned retrieval and abstention tested on a feature branch

architecture.alt: Academis retrieval architecture showing PDF ingestion into subject-tagged chunks and MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, then a student question retrieving context for answer generation
architecture.caption: Versioned course documents feed scoped retrieval, with source references and an explicit no-evidence path.
architecture.how: PDFs become overlapping chunks with document hashes, page numbers, course and corpus versions, and embedding metadata. Atlas queries filter that scope before retrieval; the API validates returned passages again. Verified user, course, and session identity isolate conversation history. Missing evidence or retrieval failure produces an abstention rather than an unsupported answer.
decisions: Deterministic chunk identifiers and content hashes make ingestion and source provenance inspectable across document versions.
Course, corpus version, schema, and embedding-model filters prevent unrelated material from entering the answer context.
Server-generated references include source title, page, version, and chunk identifier. These identify retrieved evidence; they do not prove every generated sentence is supported.
architecture.outcome: Fourteen backend tests and client type checks passed. A small synthetic evaluation checks course/version boundaries and abstention; it does not measure live Atlas retrieval quality or real-world answer accuracy.

dateNote: v1: Feb–May 2023; v2: Jun–Oct 2024; v3: Apr–Aug 2025. The first two versions were built without AI; later versions and September 2026 updates include AI assistance.
name: FilmVault
videoAlt: FilmVault demo showing live movie data, people browsing, member picks, ratings, and saved collections
summary: Films, television, ratings, and saved collections—with live catalog data from TMDB.
detail: TMDB owns the movie catalog; FilmVault owns your ratings and collection. I revisited this earlier project to handle upstream outages and stop loading an entire collection just to show its first page. The updated client searches and sorts on the server, with bounded cursor pages.
note: Catalog resilience and pagination are merged into main. FilmVault is not currently deployed; the video is a local demo. Benchmark figures come from synthetic MySQL data, not production traffic.
bullets: Express combines TMDB search and recommendations with member-owned data.
Registration, email verification, password recovery, and JWT authorization.
MySQL in the original design, plus SQLite for repeatable local demos.
Terraform defines the original OCI infrastructure, including networking, secrets, and access controls.

ownership.scope: React client, Express API, member data, TMDB integration, and original OCI design
ownership.status: Catalog resilience and pagination merged; not currently deployed

architecture.alt: FilmVault architecture showing a React client calling an Express API that combines TMDB catalog data with member accounts, ratings, collections, email, and OCI storage
architecture.caption: Catalog metadata stays external; FilmVault owns the social layer around it.
architecture.how: React calls an Express API for catalog browsing and member-owned collections. A shared TMDB client bounds upstream requests and can explicitly return stale catalog data during eligible failures. Collection queries use validated cursors, whole-collection search, stable sort tie-breakers, and authenticated ownership checks.
decisions: Only public catalog reads enter the bounded, process-local cache. Concurrent requests coalesce; retries share a deadline and stale responses are explicitly marked.
The updated client requests cursor pagination explicitly, preserving older API formats. Search is debounced, obsolete requests are canceled, and late results cannot replace the current view.
MySQL query plans guided the pagination work. Deep pages can still scan many index entries; cursor pagination is not a constant-work guarantee.
architecture.outcome: For a 10,000-item collection, warm median database/response-construction time was 33.62 ms for a full read and 0.56 ms for the first 15 items. Initial JSON fell from 6.27 MB to 9.55 KB. MySQL, SQLite, API, and client tests cover the contracts; these are not end-to-end production timings.

dateNote: Original build without AI. Offline editing and Firebase correctness updates: September 2026, with AI assistance.
name: AnimalCalendar
summary: An animal-themed calendar with offline drafts and a plan for when two edits disagree.
detail: One of my earlier projects, revisited at the point where calendars get awkward: no connection, another tab, or an event edited elsewhere. Drafts stay in the browser until they can sync, and conflicting edits stay available for review instead of silently replacing newer data.
bullets: Account-scoped IndexedDB drafts and snapshots survive reloads and overlay pending edits on the calendar.
Reconnection checks the original event version. Concurrent edits and deletion tombstones trigger an explicit conflict instead of restoring stale data.
Operation identifiers recognize the last accepted write after an acknowledgment is lost. Conditional queue removal protects newer drafts from older completions.
Two Firebase emulator clients exercise offline edits, competing changes, deletion conflicts, and replay. Fifteen date, queue, and emulator tests passed.
note: Implemented and tested on codex/offline-conflicts; not deployed. Browser storage can be cleared or evicted, and conflicting fields are not automatically merged. Firebase rules must be updated before the new client is released.

ownership.scope: Calendar interface, authentication, event persistence, security rules, and emulator tests
ownership.status: Offline editing and conflict handling tested on a feature branch

name: Summit Tutoring Center
summary: A working website for a tutoring center, with schedules the staff can update themselves.
detail: I built this for a tutoring business owned by family friends. It covers classes, staff, counseling, and inquiries, and fits the hosting setup they already had.
bullets: Staff maintain schedules, seminars, and posts through published Google Sheets.
CSV parsing handles quoted and multiline fields, with caching and stale-data fallback.
The inquiry flow uses Web3Forms when configured and falls back to an email draft.
Deployed to the business’s existing DreamHost account.

ownership.scope: Information architecture, frontend, staff-managed content flow, and deployment

architecture.alt: Summit Tutoring Center publishing flow from staff-managed Google Sheets through CSV parsing and browser caching to the React website on DreamHost
architecture.caption: A deliberately small publishing system that the business can operate without a CMS.
architecture.how: Staff edit schedules, seminars, and posts in familiar Google Sheets. The React site fetches the published CSV, parses quoted and multiline fields, and keeps the latest good response in browser storage. The production build stays on the business's existing DreamHost account.
decisions: Google Sheets serves as the editing interface, avoiding a custom CMS and new staff accounts.
A five-minute cache limits repeat fetches while stale-data fallback keeps the last valid schedule visible.
The inquiry form uses Web3Forms when configured and can fall back to an email draft.
architecture.outcome: The site is live for a real tutoring business, and nontechnical staff can update frequently changing information without asking for a code deployment.
